string.text: {=EA_ALG_desc}By 1715, the Algonquin peoples of the Ottawa River Valley and adjacent regions navigated a complex, transitional landscape shaped by the aftermath of the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701 and the conclusion of Queen Anne's War in 1713. Secure from the devastating, systematic Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) raids of the previous century, Algonquin bands operated within a stabilized geopolitical framework, maintaining their traditional seasonal cycles of hunting, fishing, and gathering while expanding their pivotal role as middleman traders in the French fur trade network. However, this period of relative peace brought its own pressures; the intensified focus on the fur trade altered their traditional subsistence economy, increased their reliance on European trade goods, and accelerated cultural changes as Catholic missions, such as those at Sillery and later Lake of the Two Mountains, concentrated populations and deeply influenced local social structures.
